nameStory: The Luna moth gets its magical name from Luna, the Roman goddess of the moon, inspired by its pale, ethereal appearance and nocturnal habits. Those distinctive crescent-shaped eyespots on its wings also evoke the phases of the moon. Early naturalists were captivated by this ghostly green giant that seemed to embody moonlight itself.
description: The Luna moth is one of North America's most spectacular and largest moths, with a wingspan that can reach up to 4.5 inches across. Its wings are a striking pale lime-green color, decorated with transparent "window" eyespots and elegant, flowing tails on the hindwings that can be several inches long. The body is thick and fuzzy, colored white with some green tinges, and the antennae are feathery and prominent. These nocturnal beauties are active at night and are often drawn to outdoor lights during their brief adult lives.

idTips.label: Lime-green wings
idTips.description: Large, pale lime-green wings that feel powdery to the touch, almost like velvet dusted with fine powder that can rub off on your fingers

idTips.label: Long hindwing tails
idTips.description: Distinctive curved tails extending from the back wings that can be 2-3 inches long and flutter gracefully when the moth moves

idTips.label: Transparent eyespots
idTips.description: Clear, window-like circular spots on each wing that look like transparent glass set into the green wing fabric

idTips.label: Feathery antennae
idTips.description: Thick, plume-like antennae that feel soft and delicate, resembling tiny ferns or feathers when examined closely

idTips.label: Massive size
idTips.description: Impressive wingspan up to 4.5 inches makes this moth impossible to mistake for anything smaller - about the size of your outstretched hand

idTips.label: Fuzzy white body
idTips.description: Thick, densely furry body that's primarily white with green edges, feeling soft and plush like a small stuffed animal

habitat: Luna moths are found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, particularly where their host trees grow abundantly. Look for them in areas with birch, hickory, walnut, sweet gum, and persimmon trees, as the caterpillars feed exclusively on these species. They're most commonly encountered in suburban areas with mature shade trees and near forest edges where outdoor lighting might attract the nocturnal adults.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring (May-June) for their first brood, often found resting on tree bark or near outdoor lights in the early morning hours.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in summer when adults are most active at night, and caterpillars can be found feeding on host tree leaves. A second brood of adults may emerge in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Caterpillars pupate in fall, spinning cocoons among leaf litter on the ground where they'll overwinter as pupae.
seasonality.winter: Only pupae survive the winter, hidden in protective cocoons buried in leaf litter and soil, waiting for spring warmth to trigger emergence.

funFact: Adult Luna moths don't have mouths or digestive systems - they literally cannot eat and survive only on the fat stores they built up as caterpillars, living just one week to mate and lay eggs before dying of starvation.
confusionNotes: Luna moths are occasionally confused with other large green moths, but the combination of lime-green color, long hindwing tails, and massive size makes them unmistakable. Remember: "Luna = long tails" - no other large green moth in New England has those distinctive flowing hindwing extensions.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "luna" moths, they're actually most active during the darkest parts of the night, not necessarily when the moon is visible. The adults you find during the day are usually exhausted from their nighttime activities and may appear sluggish or motionless.
compareHints: Luna moths are the only species in their genus (Actias) found in New England, making them unique in the region. Within their family of giant silk moths, they're easily distinguished from Cecropia moths by their green color and tail extensions, and from Polyphemus moths by their much larger size and distinctive tails. No other large moth in our region combines that ethereal lime-green color with such dramatic hindwing extensions.
